title: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework: Bearer Token Usage
subtitle: How a client shows an OAuth access token to an API, and what the API says when the token is wrong.
summary: RFC 6750 defines the "Bearer" way of using an OAuth 2.0 access token: whoever holds the token can use it, with no extra proof. It specifies three ways to send the token in an HTTP request (an Authorization header, a form body field, or a URI query parameter), how a server answers with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer challenge, and three error codes. Because possession is all that counts, it requires TLS and spends much of its length on keeping tokens from leaking.

eli5.summary: A bearer token is like a movie ticket: anyone holding it gets in, so you must keep it safe and only show it at the right door. This document says how to hand the ticket over and what the guard says if it is wrong.

questions: how do i send an oauth access token in an http request
what does www-authenticate bearer invalid_token mean
why should access tokens not be put in the url
what is the difference between invalid_token and insufficient_scope

tldr.problem: OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) issues access tokens but leaves open how a client presents one to the server that holds the protected data.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends the token with the "Bearer" scheme, preferably in the Authorization header, over TLS. The server replies to bad requests with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer challenge carrying an error code.
tldr.outcome: Almost every OAuth 2.0 API uses this header form today. The cost is that a stolen token works for anyone, which later work such as sender-constrained tokens tries to reduce.

today: This is the form of authorization you meet in most web APIs: a request with Authorization: Bearer ... and a 401 carrying WWW-Authenticate: Bearer when it fails. The header method is also what OpenID Connect UserInfo endpoints and countless JSON APIs accept. The query-parameter method is widely discouraged and the form-body method is rare. Newer guidance, RFC 9700, updates this RFC, and DPoP (RFC 9449) and mutual-TLS bound tokens (RFC 8705) add proof of possession on top of the same header.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
OAuth lets a client reach a protected resource without holding the resource owner's password. Instead an authorization server issues an access token, which RFC 6749 defines as "a string representing an access authorization issued to the client". This RFC covers the last two steps of the abstract flow: the client presents the token to the resource server (step E) and the server validates it and serves the request (step F).

It does this for one kind of token, the bearer token, over HTTP/1.1 with TLS. The RFC notes that although it was written for OAuth 2.0 flows, it actually defines a general HTTP authorization method that works with bearer tokens from any source. It also puts some semantic requirements on the token returned in step D.

The RFC sits next to RFC 6749, which defines how tokens are obtained. This one only covers how they are used.
sections.eli5: Getting a ticket is one job and showing it at the door is another. This document is only about showing it at the door.

sections.title: What a bearer token is
sections.content:
The RFC defines a bearer token as a security token with the property that any party in possession of it (a "bearer") can use it in any way that any other holder can. A bearer does not have to prove possession of cryptographic key material.

That makes tokens easy to use: the resource server needs no knowledge of passwords or other login methods, only of the token, and tokens can be short-lived. It also makes them dangerous, because a copied token works as well as the original. The abstract says it plainly: to prevent misuse, bearer tokens need to be protected from disclosure in storage and in transport.
sections.eli5: Think of cash or a concert ticket. The guard does not ask whose it is. That is simple, but if someone steals it, they can use it.

sections.title: Sending the token
sections.content:
Section 2 of the RFC defines three ways to send a bearer token, and a client MUST NOT use more than one in a single request.

The Authorization header carries Authorization: Bearer mF_9.B5f-4.1JqM. The credentials are the word "Bearer", one or more spaces, and a b64token: letters, digits, and the characters - . _ ~ + /, followed by any number of =. Clients SHOULD use this method and resource servers MUST support it.

The form-encoded body puts access_token=... in a POST body. It is allowed only if the Content-Type is application/x-www-form-urlencoded, the body is single-part and entirely ASCII, and the method has defined body semantics (so never GET). It SHOULD NOT be used unless browsers cannot set the Authorization header. Servers MAY support it.

The URI query parameter puts ?access_token=... in the URL. The RFC says it is included "to document current use" and is not recommended, because URLs are routinely logged. Clients using it SHOULD send Cache-Control: no-store.
sections.eli5: There are three places to show your ticket: hold it up at the front (the header), tuck it into the note you hand over (the body), or write its number on the outside of the envelope (the URL). The first is best; the last is risky because everyone who handles the envelope can read it.

sections.title: The WWW-Authenticate challenge
sections.content:
When a request has no credentials or an unusable token, the resource server MUST send a WWW-Authenticate response header. Every challenge from this RFC uses the auth-scheme Bearer followed by one or more auth-params.

The attributes are realm (scope of protection, at most once), scope (a space-delimited list of case-sensitive scope values the token needs, at most once, meant for programs rather than people), and, when a token was supplied and failed, error (SHOULD be included), error_description and error_uri (both MAY, each at most once). Other auth-params are allowed.

If the request carried no authentication information at all, the server SHOULD NOT include an error code, because the client may simply not have known authentication was needed. The bare challenge is WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="example".
sections.eli5: If you show the wrong ticket, or none, the guard tells you which kind of ticket the door wants and, if you showed one, what was wrong with it.

sections.title: Error codes
sections.content:
Section 3.1 of the RFC defines three error values, each paired with a recommended HTTP status. Responses are typically 400, 401, 403 or 405.

invalid_request
Missing or repeated parameter, unsupported value, more than one token method used, or otherwise malformed. SHOULD be 400.
invalid_token
Expired, revoked, malformed or otherwise invalid. SHOULD be 401. The client MAY get a new token and retry.
insufficient_scope
The token is valid but too weak. SHOULD be 403, and the server MAY include the needed scope.

The RFC registers all three in the OAuth Extensions Error registry, and registers "Bearer" in the OAuth Access Token Types registry defined by RFC 6749.
sections.eli5: The guard has three standard answers: "your ticket is smudged", "your ticket is no good any more", and "your ticket is real, but not for this room".

sections.title: Getting a token
sections.content:
Section 4 of the RFC shows what the token usually looks like when it arrives, as part of an RFC 6749 access token response. It is a 200 OK JSON object with access_token, token_type set to Bearer, expires_in in seconds (3600 in the example), and an optional refresh_token. The response carries Cache-Control: no-store and Pragma: no-cache.

The token_type value is how the client knows it must use this specification's rules for the token. The RFC says nothing about what the token string contains; it may be a signed structure or just an unguessable reference that the resource server looks up.
sections.eli5: When the office hands you a ticket, the slip it comes with says what kind of ticket it is and how long it lasts.

sections.title: Security considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists four threats taken from NIST SP 800-63: token manufacture or modification, token disclosure, token redirect (a token for one resource server used at another) and token replay. The main defences are:

Safeguarding the token is the primary security consideration. Clients MUST always use TLS, MUST validate the certificate chain, and MUST NOT store bearer tokens in cookies that can be sent in the clear.

Token servers SHOULD issue short-lived tokens (one hour or less) with an audience restriction, so a leaked token does little. Token contents must be protected against modification, for example with a signature or MAC, or the token can be an unguessable reference. Where TLS ends at a load balancer, the hop to the back end MUST also be protected. Tokens SHOULD NOT go in page URLs, because browser history and server logs may keep them. A summary of these recommendations closes the section.
sections.eli5: Keep the ticket in your pocket, show it only at the real door, and prefer tickets that expire soon, so a lost one is not a big problem.

data.code:
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="example",
                  error="invalid_token",
                  error_description="The access token expired"

  "access_token":"mF_9.B5f-4.1JqM",

  "refresh_token":"tGzv3JOkF0XG5Qx2TlKWIA"
}

items.title: Always TLS
items.text: Use https and validate the certificate chain on every request that carries a token.

items.title: Short-lived tokens
items.text: Token servers SHOULD issue tokens valid for one hour or less.

items.title: Audience and scope
items.text: Restrict tokens to the intended resource servers so a redirected token is useless elsewhere.

items.title: Keep out of URLs and cookies
items.text: URLs end up in logs and history; cookies sent in the clear expose the token.
